subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: Dear Tushar, Thank you for helping with the science project last week. I have been thinking about the day we took the bus to the lab. You had to leave home at five to get there on time, and you mentioned it as if it was nothing. I get dropped by car, and I have never once wondered how I would get anywhere. I also realised that I have had a tutor since class six and a quiet room at home, and I always thought that was just normal for everybody. I don't feel bad, exactly. I feel more awake, and more thankful. I would like to be fairer. Next time I could help with the lab report, and share my old notebooks if you find them useful. Only if you want to. Nirmala

qa.q: At what time did Tushar leave home to reach the lab?
qa.a: Tushar had to leave home at five to get there on time.

qa.q: How does Nirmala feel about this realisation?
qa.a: Nirmala feels more awake and thankful, not guilty. Nirmala says "I don't feel bad, exactly" and wants to be fairer.

qa.q: What choice does Nirmala make in the letter after seeing the difference?
qa.a: Nirmala offers to help with the lab report and share old notebooks, but only if Tushar wants, so the offer stays respectful.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel on receiving the letter?
qa.a: Possibly surprised, and pleased to be noticed. Because the offer is optional, Tushar can accept it without feeling pitied. 🙂

grounding: A teenager from a comfortable background notices advantages that others lack, feels thankfulness rather than guilt, and wants to act fairly.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage: So on the school radio show they asked, what changed how you see things this year? For me it was Afreen. She topped the maths test, and I asked if she wanted to revise at my place, and she said she had to catch the six-ten bus, because there's no later one. I had always thought everyone had a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Afreen does her homework on a shared table with her little brothers. That day I realised that my marks come partly from my things. I don't think that's something to feel guilty about. It just means I should say thank you at home, and make sure Afreen gets the same practice papers I get. We share them now, and she explains the tricky ones better than my tutor does. Shankar

qa.q: What bus did Afreen have to catch?
qa.a: Afreen had to catch the six-ten bus, because there is no later one.

qa.q: What did Shankar realise that day, and how does Shankar feel about it?
qa.a: Shankar realised that the marks come partly from having a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Shankar feels thankful and more aware, not guilty.

qa.q: Which choice did Shankar make after realising this?
qa.a: Shankar decided to say thank you at home and to share the same practice papers with Afreen, so both have equal practice.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the sharing of practice papers?
qa.a: Afreen probably sees it as fair and friendly, since she also explains the tricky ones and helps in return, so it is exchange and not charity.

grounding: A teenager from a comfortable background sees that ease comes with advantages others lack, and responds with thanks and fairness instead of guilt.
